title: Service Mesh Security
summary: Service mesh security is the practice of enforcing identity, encryption and access rules between workloads through a dedicated infrastructure layer that sits beside the application. In a mesh, each service instance gets a sidecar or node-level proxy that intercepts network traffic, and a control plane distributes policy to those proxies. The important consequence is that the mesh issues a cryptographic identity to each workload and can require mutual authentication, so both sides of a connection prove who they are with short-lived certificates rather than trusting an address inside a shared network. Policy then answers which service may call which endpoint, on which path or method, and telemetry records every allowed and denied connection. This matters most in clusters where many teams share one flat network and any pod could otherwise reach any other. The frequent mistake is treating a mesh as a complete security product and forgetting that it does not fix a compromised workload, a leaked secret or an over-privileged role, and that policy left in a permissive monitoring mode silently allows what the team believes it blocks.

beginner.definition: A service mesh is a layer of small helper programs that sit next to your services. They manage the traffic between those services. Service mesh security uses that layer to prove identity, encrypt connections and allow only approved calls.
beginner.whyItMatters: In a shared cluster, many programs run on the same network and can often reach each other freely. One weak program can then talk to a sensitive one without asking. The mesh makes every program prove who it is before a call is allowed. It also encrypts traffic inside the cluster and records who talked to whom.
howItWorks: A small helper program is placed next to each service in the cluster.
A central control plane gives every service a cryptographic identity and a certificate.
Those certificates are short-lived and then renewed automatically, without any human work.
When one service calls another, both sides prove their identity before traffic flows.
Policy rules state which service may call which address, path or action.
The helpers record every allowed and every denied connection for later review.
beginner.example: Picture an apartment building where every flat door opens with the same key, so any neighbour can enter any flat. Now imagine each resident receives a key that opens only their own door and the shared laundry. When someone knocks, the resident checks an identity card before opening. A service mesh gives each program its own key and puts a careful doorman at every door. Even inside the building, a visitor must show who they are and be expected before entering.
takeaways: The mesh gives each workload an identity, so trust no longer depends on network address.
Test policy in a monitoring mode before you enforce it, or you will block real traffic.
A mesh does not fix a compromised workload or a leaked secret by itself.

objectives: Explain what a service mesh is and where its proxies sit in the traffic path.
Describe how workload identity and mutual authentication replace network trust.
Interpret a mesh authorisation policy that restricts which service may call an endpoint.
Explain why short-lived certificates reduce the risk of credential theft.
Recognise the limits of a mesh when a workload itself is compromised.
